text:
Recent annotation research supports explicit decision rules, evidence capture and disagreement audits. A [2025 study of annotation disagreement](https://aclanthology.org/2025.comedi-1.3/) found that task wording and annotator selection change instance-level labels; preference comparisons were not demonstrably higher quality than individual ratings. [Annotating the Annotators (2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.922/) found that inter-annotator agreement alone inadequately assessed correctness, supporting error-specific audits and expert oversight. These findings support piloting a codebook and retaining original labels and rationales before adjudication; they do not establish a validated recommendation-specific five-state taxonomy.

Suggested application: start with the twenty training-user recommendation lists and annotate each available feedback statement on separate dimensions: immediate choice, general interest, explicit deferral, explicit mismatch and insufficient information. Interest and deferral can coexist. Attach the exact supporting feedback span to every substantive label; distinguish missing evidence from an explicit request for more information. Ownership, compatibility and intent remain unknown unless feedback explicitly establishes them; title or description similarity cannot establish these user facts. Independently double-code the small sample, report per-dimension agreement and nominal Krippendorff’s alpha, inspect confusion patterns, and record abstention rates and evidence-support errors. Preserve unresolved ambiguity rather than force negative labels. This is a proposed diagnostic protocol informed by annotation research, not an empirically validated taxonomy or a second predictor; use its findings to describe auditable failure hypotheses, while retaining macro validation HR@10 for model selection.
